A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same graph convolutional deep kernel machine research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original node- and graph-classification experiments, regularization sweeps, and additional baseline results in Appendix A.3.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification benchmarks, kernel-alignment measurements, numerical verification of its linear solution, and inducing-point and depth analyses.

M1.justification: The core graph-DKM objective is retained, but v2 adds an intra-domain inducing-point scheme alongside v1's isolated-node scheme. Appendices B/C explicitly introduce a different classification output layer using sampled weights, while Appendix I proposes factorized Nyström propagation. Kernel centering and modified adjacency options further extend the procedure.

E1.justification: Node-classification coverage expands from nine to fourteen datasets through Reddit, Arxiv, Penn94, Flickr, and BlogCatalog. Enzymes is removed, reducing graph-classification coverage from six datasets to five. v2 also introduces synthetic Erdős–Rényi graphs for studying representations under random graph structure.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds systematic GCN-without-dropout test comparisons; v1 only reports a dropout comparison for Roman Empire in its discussion. The core GCN and NNGP comparators remain. Sparse and full-rank NNGPs were already represented across v1 Tables 3 and 5, so their consolidation is not a new comparator.

E3.justification: Appendix E replaces v1's hyperparameter searches with four sequential sweeps, changes inducing-point counts and GCN widths, and fixes final benchmark depth at two layers. Preprocessing, training budgets, and learning-rate schedules are revised, including warmup followed by cosine decay. New representation analyses introduce CKA measurements and additional experimental controls.

E4.justification: v2 adds analytic-versus-trained kernel verification, adjacency-interpolation sensitivity, kernel-alignment analysis, inducing-scheme comparisons, and depth sweeps. The node regularization study is revised, while v1's graph-classification regularization curves and homophily-versus-relative-improvement analysis are removed. These substantially change the questions investigated beyond benchmark accuracy.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations. v2 adds standard-deviation bands to the regularization plots and specifies split-mean aggregation in Table 1. It omits v1's explicit final 20-seed/50-run counts and homophily–improvement significance test; these omissions do not establish that fewer runs were performed.

E6.justification: Results change broadly under revised settings. For example, DKM accuracy on Roman Empire changes from 75.6±0.7 to 79.2±0.4, and on NCI1 from 71.0±0.7 to 75.3±1.0 (v1 Tables 3–4; v2 Tables 1–2). New benchmark and analysis results are added, while Enzymes results disappear. These are replacement results, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: v2 adds full-rank and sparse objective derivations, generalizes the inducing-node kernel derivation, and derives a closed-form linear graph-DKM solution with a validity argument in Section 5 and Appendix D. These go substantially beyond v1's kernel calculations. However, new Appendix A equations 22 and 24 use a positive KL term, inconsistent with the negative term in the main objective.

C1.justification: v2 adds explicit contributions for two inducing-point schemes and a closed-form analysis of learned representations. Its abstract and contribution list focus on homophily-dependent node-classification benefits rather than v1's claim that representation learning is necessary for both heterophilous node and graph classification. Graph classification remains supporting experimental evidence.

C2.justification: v2 develops explanations based on kernel alignment, rank collapse, adjacency mixing, and compensation for unsuitable inductive biases. It broadens the dropout explanation using new controls and discusses inducing-scheme applicability. The new limitations section explicitly restricts conclusions to standard graph-convolutional architectures and considers how alternative architectural biases could particularly benefit NNGPs.

D1.justification: Appendices E–I substantially expand documentation of training sweeps, batching, preprocessing, numerical-stability workarounds, centering, and parameterization. Some information is lost, including v1's explicit graph train/validation/test proportions. New details also conflict: Figure 1 specifies 100 Cora nodes, whereas Appendices D.2 and E.4 specify 200.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused positioning against homophily research, including Luan, Zhu, and Maurya, and references supporting kernel alignment, oversmoothing, and added datasets. It distinguishes studying representation learning from studying homophily's effect on GNN performance. The central positioning relative to NNGPs, NTKs, and DKMs remains intact.

P1.justification: The background and experimental narrative are substantially rewritten and reorganized. Dataset descriptions move out of the main experimental overview, inducing-point methods receive a main-text subsection, limitations become a separate section, and appendix organization changes extensively. The title is also shortened.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. v1's grouped regularization plot becomes separate dataset panels with uncertainty bands, its improvement scatterplot disappears, and v2 adds kernel heatmaps, a loss curve, and depth plots. Results tables gain comparator columns, dataset-statistics tables move to the appendix, and an inducing-scheme table is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central representation-learning argument through systematic dropout controls, direct kernel-alignment measurements, broader benchmark coverage, and inducing-point and depth analyses. These address v1's reliance mainly on accuracy sweeps and a conjectured dropout explanation. Missing run counts, conflicting experimental details, and Appendix A's KL-sign inconsistency weaken reproducibility and mathematical presentation, but the stronger empirical support and clearer applicability limits provide a substantial net improvement.
